spots.name: Livraria Lello
spots.label: Livraria Lello

text.access_note: This is a ticketed bookshop, and entry has been charged since 2015, so check the official site before you go for current entry and photo rules.
text.geographic_location: Livraria Lello is in central Porto, on Rua das Carmelitas, facing the Praça de Lisboa. It is a short stroll from the Clérigos Church and tower and close to the University of Porto's Faculty of Sciences building.
text.description: Livraria Lello is a bookshop that opened in 1906 on Rua das Carmelitas, and it is one of the oldest bookshops in Portugal. It is often ranked among the best in the world. It photographs well because the building is full of detail, outside and in. The facade mixes Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau touches. Painted figures representing Art and Science sit above the entrance arch, with the firm's name in bright lettering and small pinnacles along the top. Inside, a forked staircase curves up to a wooden-balustraded gallery. Above it is a large stained glass window measuring 8 by 3.5 metres, carrying the motto Decus in Labore. The ceilings and walls are painted plaster made to look like carved wood, and the small rails and wooden cart once used to move books between the shelves are still there. For your phone, there are two kinds of picture here. Outside, you want the whole front, and then close crops of the painted figures and pinnacles. Inside, you want the staircase, the stained glass and the curved lines of the gallery. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. Entry to the shop has been charged since 2015, so check the official site before you go, including what is allowed for photos inside. It can get busy, so be patient when waiting for a clear view of the staircase.
text.directions_text: Head for the Clérigos Church and tower, which are near the bookshop, then walk to the Praça de Lisboa, where the bookshop faces onto Rua das Carmelitas. The phone icon on the map is at the bookshop itself, so once you reach the front door you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the facade from here, stepping back only as far as you need to fit the whole front in the shot. For the interior, stand near the foot of the forked staircase, if the queue and the rules on the day allow it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer, with fewer people in your frame. The facade faces south, so it is likely to be in direct sun around midday.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stained glass window to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the glass does not wash out. If the interior is dim, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in from where you stand, and for the staircase inside. Use the default lens (1x) for general views and details such as the balusters. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the painted figures and pinnacles above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade's edges up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. For the staircase, hold the phone upright, centre the curve of the steps and include some of the stained glass at the top. Then take a closer shot of the painted figures above the entrance arch, using the telephoto lens.

spots.name: Porto Cathedral
spots.label: Porto Cathedral

text.access_note: The square is open at all hours and free, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements inside.
text.geographic_location: Porto Cathedral stands in the historic centre of Porto, on the square called Terreiro da Sé, which is in front of its main façade.
text.description:
Porto Cathedral is a Roman Catholic church in the old centre of the city. It is one of Porto's oldest buildings and one of its most important Romanesque ones. It was built on the site of an old chapel or hermitage founded in 1108. The present church was begun in the second half of the 12th century, and work carried on until the 16th. The 18th century then brought major Baroque changes, including a new main portal in 1772 and a loggia by Nicolau Nasoni on the side façade in 1736. King John I married Philippa of Lancaster here in 1387.

It photographs well because of its shape. Two square towers topped with cupolas flank a plain, heavy front with a Romanesque rose window under a crenellated arch, so the whole building looks a little like a fortress. That makes the classic postcard view.

Keep the phone level and let the towers fill the upper part of the picture, with the cross low in the frame. The square gets busy, so go early if you want it clear of people. If you have time, the sloping street Calçada Dom Pedro Pitões gives a closer, steeper view of the towers above the rooftops.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the historic centre of Porto and ask for Terreiro da Sé, the square in front of the cathedral. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Terreiro da Sé (right-hand corner of the square, facing the cathedral front). The cathedral's twin-towered façade in the background, with a stone cross in the middle of the square in the foreground. In the right-hand corner of the square, facing the cathedral front. From here you see the twin-towered façade in the background, with the stone cross in the middle of the square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the square fills up with other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus and drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the full twin-towered façade and the stone cross in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and tower tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the phone upright so the towers stay straight. Put the cross low in the frame as a lead-in, with the façade filling the upper two thirds. For a second picture, try the sloping street Calçada Dom Pedro Pitões, which gives a closer view of the towers above the old-town roofs.

text.access_note: This is a working market and may have set opening days, hours and rules for visitors, so check the official site before you go.
text.description:
Bolhão Market is a market in Porto and is ranked 3 on the Porto shot map. It is a good place for lively, colourful phone photos. Depending on the day, you might find stacked fruit and vegetables, flower stalls, fish counters, hand-written signs and stallholders at work. The phone icon on the map sits at the market itself, so you can start shooting as soon as you arrive.

Work in layers. Take one wide shot to show the setting and the crowd. Then step closer for a single stall, a pile of produce or a price sign. Markets are busy places, so keep moving gently, stay out of the way of people shopping and carrying goods, and ask politely before pointing your phone at a stallholder's face. Many people are happy to be photographed if you smile and ask first.

Light in a market can vary between bright and shaded areas. Tap on the part of the scene you care about most and nudge the exposure slider until the food looks natural rather than washed out. If you want a quiet frame without people, arriving early or at a slower moment of the day usually helps. Rules about photography, opening days and which areas are open to visitors can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Navigate to the coordinates or search for 'Bolhão Market' in your maps app. Once you are there, the phone icon on the map is at the market itself, so there is no extra walk to the photo spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Once you arrive, look around for a spot with a clear view that keeps you out of people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings are usually the liveliest time for stalls and activity, while a quieter period gives cleaner shots with fewer people in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the food or the face you want sharp, then slide the exposure down a little if bright areas are washing out the picture. Night mode may kick in automatically in dim areas, so hold the phone steady against your body or a rail for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for stalls and street scenes. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for wide scenes, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details and faces from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a stall, a flower display or a sign on one of the lines. Keep the ultra-wide close to your subject and watch the edges, because it can stretch people and straight lines. For food, fill the frame with colour and shoot slightly from above.
